question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is probably 4. When recognizing PLL after OLL in CFOP you mainly need to distinguish the permutation of the four last-layer edges (and confirm the corners match), so seeing one side sticker per edge—visible on the front and right faces for example—gives you the four key references without needing the top layer. That’s usually enough to tell apart the 21 cases once you’ve memorized the patterns, though a few tricky ones like G-perms might benefit from an extra glance.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is probably 5. When recognizing PLL you typically need to distinguish both edge cycles and corner cycles on the U layer. A common efficient approach is to inspect the four side-facing edge stickers (which immediately shows whether you have a pure edge swap, adjacent swap, or diagonal case) plus one additional side-facing corner sticker to resolve the corner permutation without ambiguity. That totals five non-top-facing stickers and covers all 21 cases in practice, since the remaining orientations follow from the visible colors relative to the fixed centers.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is 4. To identify the PLL case on a 3x3, examining two adjacent side faces is typically enough, which shows the four vertical stickers belonging to the last-layer edges. Those four stickers immediately reveal the edge permutation cycle structure (and by extension the corners), without any need to rotate the cube further or peek at additional faces. This matches what most CFOP solvers do in one look during recognition.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is probably 5. In CFOP, PLL recognition on the last layer relies on distinguishing the 21 cases by the side colors of the U-layer edges and corners (the non-U stickers). You generally need to confirm the positions of all four edges plus at least one corner to rule out the similar cases like the G-perms versus the U-perms or A-perms. That totals five stickers visible from the sides; seeing only four often leaves an ambiguity between two cases that share the same edge cycle but differ in corner twist or swap. Once those five match a known pattern you can execute the alg without further inspection.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is 4. In CFOP PLL recognition, the last-layer permutation is fully determined by the relative positions of the U-layer edges and corners to the centers. Because the four U-layer edges each expose exactly one non-U sticker, examining those four side stickers (typically by viewing two adjacent faces) gives you the full cycle structure for both edges and corners—any remaining ambiguity is resolved by the fixed centers and the fact that corners must follow the same permutation parity. This is why experienced solvers can call cases like Aa/Ab or E with only a quick two-face glance covering four stickers total.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe 5 non-top-facing stickers are sufficient. With OLL complete, the four equatorial side stickers on the U-layer edges immediately reveal most edge permutations, and one carefully chosen corner side sticker (for instance on UFR) is enough to resolve the remaining corner cycles and distinguish the 21 cases; the final piece is fixed by parity, so an extra sticker is redundant.

8.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished by OLL so that the nine U stickers are all
the same colour and carry no information at all about the permutation.
All of the information which is still missing is carried by the side
stickers of the four U edges and the four U corners.

A U edge has one U sticker and one side sticker, a U corner has one U
sticker and two side stickers.  Hence on the U layer there are

* 4 edges × 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

$4+8=12$ non-U stickers in all belonging to the U layer.  Those are the
only stickers that can possibly distinguish one PLL permutation from
another.  In particular the whole D face and the three inner rows of F,
R, B and L are irrelevant for PLL.

Of course the permutation of the U layer is completely determined long
before you have actually looked at all twelve of those stickers.  The
fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity so that three
independently identifiable edges and three independently identifiable
corners, i.e. six well chosen non-U stickers, already distinguish the
21 essentially different PLL permutations, and the usual “one identifier
per U piece’’ textbook count is the eight identifiers, i.e. the twelve
physical side stickers of the U layer.  It is this twelve-sticker set
which is normally quoted as the information-bearing part of the last
layer.

3.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face monochromatic.  All of the
information which distinguishes one PLL from another is therefore
contained in the side colours of the eight U-slab pieces.

The U-slab is

* 4 U edges.  An U edge shows on the U face and on just one side face,
so it contributes one non-U sticker to the information you have to
read.  4 × 1 = 4 side stickers.

* 4 U corners.  A U corner shows on the U face and on two side faces,
so it contributes two non-U stickers.  4 × 2 = 8 side stickers.

Hence the U-slab contains
4 + 8 = 12 non-U stickers in total, 4 edge side colours and 8 corner
side colours.  That is the information set of a PLL.  In practice one
side colour per piece is informationally enough to tell the piece, i.e.
one side colour for each of the four edges and one side colour for each
of the four corners, eight distinct non-U colours, the fourth edge and
the fourth corner being forced by parity.  It is this 12-sticker
U-slab, 8 distinct pieces worth, that is normally quoted as the PLL
read-out.

2.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face oriented. The U face is therefore
informationless : the 8 U stickers are all the same colour and the
permutation of the last layer is carried entirely by the side colours of
the 8 U layer cubies.

On the U layer there are

* 4 U edges.  An U edge is $U\!+\!s$ with one side sticker $s$.
* 4 U corners.  An U corner is $U\!+\!s_{1}\!+\!s_{2}$ with two side
stickers $s_{1},s_{2}$.

Hence the U layer carries

$4\times1+4\times2 = 12$

physical non-U stickers, 4 edge stickers and 8 corner stickers.  One
side sticker per U cubie is enough to tell the cubie apart from the other
three cubies of the same type, so in the usual "one face per cubie"
language you have to be able to name the 4 U edges and the 4 U corners,
i.e. 8 distinct U-layer pieces.  In information theoretic terms the
four edge permutation and the four corner permutation have the same
parity, so the permutation of the whole U layer is fixed by the
information carried in seven of the twelve side stickers, the eighth
being a parity check.  In practice this is phrased as the 8 U-layer
pieces, the 4 edge side stickers and the 4 corners, i.e. the 12 side
stickers of the U layer, 7 of which are information-theoretically
necessary.  The conventional statement is that the PLL is carried by the
eight U cubies, four edge side stickers and four corners, i.e. the 12
non-U stickers of the U layer, normally quoted as the eight pieces
$4+4$ that can be read with seven independent side stickers.

*Remark.*  If you count physical stickers the U layer has 12 non-U
stickers.  The 7–8 sticker form is the usual cubing shorthand: 4 edge
side stickers and, up to parity, 3 fully identified corners, i.e. the
eight U pieces.  This is the  six-sticker view you actually get from a
single front–right view of the cube, $UF,UFL,UFR$ on the front and
$UR, UFR, UBR$ on the right, and enough to name any of the 21 PLL
classes. ∎

10.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already colour solved after OLL.  The whole
U-layer is therefore

* 4 U-corners, each of which brings two stickers into the non-U faces,
* 4 U-edges, each of which brings one sticker into a non-U face,

on the U-slice

* 4×2 = 8 corner-side stickers,
* 4×1 = 4 edge-side stickers,

so 12 stickers of the cube which are not on U belong to the
U-slice.  The absolute identity of a U-corner is the unordered pair of
its two side colours and the absolute identity of a U-edge is the
colour of its single side sticker.  Hence a complete literal description
of the U-slice permutation, i.e. the complete literal description of a
PLL, is the 12-tuple

UFR,F,R ; UFL,F,L ; ULB,U,L,B ; UBR,U,B,R  and
UF,F ; UR,R ; UB,B ; UL,L

of side colours.  That is the 12 non-U stickers of the U-slice.  Of
course the 21 PLL types are recognised in practice with a very much
smaller amount of information – the fourth corner and the fourth edge
are forced by parity and by the fixed U-colour, so six to eight well
chosen side stickers of the U-slice already separate the 21 classes.
It is the 12 side stickers of the U-slice, 8 corner side stickers + 4
edge side stickers, which carry the whole U-permutation information.
This is the 8 pieces of the U-layer that are normally spoken of as the
“8 stickers’’ of PLL recognition.

12.text:
In CFOP the U–face is finished by OLL so that the 9 U–stickers are
monochromatic. The U–face itself therefore carries no information
about the permutation which is what a PLL is. What you read is the
side–colour of the 8 U–cubies.

On the U–ring there are

* 4 U–edges, 1 side sticker per edge,
* 4 U–corners, 2 side stickers per corner,

i.e. 4+2×4 = 12 non-U stickers which belong to the last layer, 8
cubies in all.  That is the whole U ring that is normally read from
above.  In information theoretic terms the eighth cubie is forced by
the parity of the last layer, so 7 of the 8 cubies determine the PLL.
In the usual 4 edge + 3 corner optimum this is four edge side stickers
and three corners with their two side stickers each, ten side stickers
in all, normally quoted as the 7-cubie/7–sticker minimum for the
permutation.  The ring is normally just read as a whole, i.e. the 12
side stickers of the U layer, 8 cubies, of which 7 are information
theoretically sufficient.

11.text:
In CFOP the OLL is already done so the U-face is a solid colour.  The
only thing that can still change in the last layer is the permutation of
the eight U-layer cubies

* 4 U-edges, 1 side sticker per edge seen from the side of the cube
* 4 U-corners, 2 side stickers per corner seen from the side of the cube

and the D face is never used for PLL recognition.  Hence the whole
PLL information is contained in the side colouring of the U-layer.  The
U-layer has

* 4 edges $\times$ 1 side sticker = 4 , 
* 4 corners $\times$ 2 side stickers = 8

i.e. 12 non-U stickers, 8 distinct U-layer pieces, on the top layer.
In information theoretic terms one identifying sticker per piece is
enough, so the permutation of the last layer is carried by eight
identifying stickers, viz. the four edge side stickers and one side
sticker per corner.  Counting both sides of a corner the conventional
text book count is the twelve side stickers of the U-layer, 4+8, which
is the whole non-U colouring of the last layer.  This is the zero-D-
face information that is normally quoted as “the eight U-layer pieces’’
and in the usual 12-sticker counting.  The U stickers themselves carry
no information after OLL.

4.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already colour–uniform after the OLL so the top nine
stickers carry no information at all.  Everything that has to be read is
the ring that surrounds the U-face

* 4 U-edges : one non-U sticker per edge,
* 4 U-corners : two non-U stickers per corner.

That is 4+8 =12 physical side stickers on the U–slice, i.e. the eight
different U–layer pieces

* 4 edges  $E_{UF},E_{UR},E_{UB},E_{UL}$,
* 4 corners $C_{UFR},C_{URB},C_{UBL},C_{ULF}$

which can be read as one identifying sticker per piece.  In ordinary
language this is quoted as the eight U–layer pieces, twelve physical
non–U stickers, the U-ring.  Up to the four–fold vertical rotation of
the cube the eight pieces are not independent – the last piece is
forced by parity – so the information–theoretic minimum is seven
independent non–U stickers, i.e. the familiar eight–piece, twelve–sticker
U-ring that is normally quoted as “the 8 stickers, 12 physical stickers,
of the last layer”.  This is the information that is actually read in
PLL recognition.

6.text:
In CFOP after the OLL step the U-face is a solid colour

```
U1 = U2 = U3 = U4 = U5 = U6 = U7 = U8 = U9
```

so the U stickers carry no information about the permutation of the
last layer.  All the information about which U-layer cubie is in which
U-layer slot is carried by the side stickers of the eight U-layer
cubies.  

On the U-layer

* a U-edge has one U sticker and one side sticker ;
* a U-corner has one U sticker and two side stickers .

Hence the U-layer carries

```
4 edges × 1 side sticker =  4
4 corners× 2 side stickers=  8
-----------------------------
                     12
```

distinct non-U stickers.  That is the information carrying set of the
PLL.  In particular a U-edge is uniquely identified by its single
side sticker and a U-corner is uniquely identified by the unordered
pair of its two side stickers, so in principle one side sticker per
cubie is enough to tell which cubie is in which slot.  One side sticker
for each of the eight U-layer cubies is therefore enough to pin down the
4-cycle / 3-cycle / 2-cycle structure of corners and edges and hence
which of the 21 PLL classes you are in.  Up to the global  C4 rotation
about the U-axis this is seven distinct stickers, the usual seven-to-
eight-sticker practical count, and the twelve side stickers of the U
layer

```
FR, FL, BR, BL, UR, UL, UB, UF   on the four corners
F,  L,  R,  B                      on the four edges
```

are the whole set of non-U information that you ever have to look at.
It is this twelve sticker, eight-cubie, side information of the top
layer that is normally quoted as “looking at the top row of the four
side faces’’ and which carries the PLL.  The eight one-per-cubie
information, i.e. the twelve side stickers of the U layer, is the
customary statement of the result.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is about what information is left after OLL in CFOP. The U face is monochromatic so its 9 stickers carry no PLL information. All PLL information is in the U-slice side colouring.

U-slice inventory:
* 4 U-edges: 1 side sticker per edge → 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 side stickers per corner → 8 non-U stickers
Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 4+8 = 12. These are the 8 U-layer cubies normally quoted as the U-ring.

Several colleagues give the same counting and stress that the 12 side stickers are the whole set that carries the permutation. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 all state the 12 physical/8 piece description and note the U face is informationless.

Information theoretic nuance repeatedly raised:
* One identifier per cubie is enough, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct identifiers.
* Parity of the U-permutation makes the fourth edge and the fourth corner forced, so 7 independent non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient, the usual textbook 7-to-8 sticker minimum. Colleagues 10,12,2,4,8 explicitly mention the 7 independent / 8 piece shorthand.

Practical recognition disagreement:
* A minority argues for a much smaller practical glance: 4 edge side stickers, sometimes +1 corner sticker = 5 stickers, sometimes 4 stickers alone is enough for most cases. Colleagues 1,7,9 argue 5; colleagues 13,14,5 argue 4 is enough in practice for distinguishing edge cycles and by parity the corners.

No prior belief to revise. Current understanding: the complete literal description of a PLL is contained in the 12 non-U stickers of the U-layer, 8 cubies. The information-theoretic minimum is 7 independent stickers / 8 identifiers, and experienced solvers often recognise cases with a 4-5 sticker glance. The unresolved tension is whether the question asks for the total information-bearing set, 12, or the minimal guaranteed sufficient set, ~7/8, vs the practical 4-5 sticker glance.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The round-0 public pool is split between a literal counting view and a practical / information-theoretic minimum view.

Literal counting consensus:
* After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the 9 U stickers carry no PLL information.
* The only information bearing part of the last layer is the U-ring: 4 U-edges each contribute 1 side sticker = 4, 4 U-corners each contribute 2 side stickers = 8. 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers belong to the U-slice, i.e. the 8 U-layer cubies. Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,10,11,12 all state this 12-sticker / 8-piece U-ring as the complete physical description of a PLL. The U stickers themselves are informationless.

Information-theoretic / practical minimum:
* Because the U colour is fixed and the edge and corner permutations have the same parity, the 8th cubie is forced. Hence the permutation is fixed by 7 independent identifiers, often phrased as 7 cubies / 7-8 identifying stickers. Colleague 2,4,12 etc. give the 7 independent / 8 piece shorthand, with a typical textbook count of 4 edge side stickers + 3 fully identified corners = 10 physical side stickers.
* A number of colleagues argue for a much smaller practical glance: 4, 5. Colleagues 1,7,9 say ~5 non-top stickers – the four edge side stickers plus one corner side sticker – is enough to break the 21 classes, with G-perms being the main reason an extra sticker is mentioned. Colleagues 13,14,5 say four edge side stickers on two adjacent faces are often enough in practice for recognition, with corner parity resolving the rest.
* Colleague 10/11 note that the absolute identity of a U-corner is an unordered pair of side colours and of a U-edge is its single side colour, so a complete literal description is the 12-tuple of side colours. The 21 PLL types can be separated with a much smaller well-chosen subset, 6-8 stickers.

Unresolved for me:
* The question wording is ambiguous between “how many non-U stickers exist on the U-layer” = 12 physical, “how many identifiers are information-theoretically necessary” = 7 independent ~8 pieces ~10-12 physical, and “how many can a human actually glance at in practice to name the 21 cases” = 4-5 stickers that many solvers claim is sufficient.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Building on what Colleague 1, 7 and 9 have already noted, five non-U stickers really does separate all 21 cases once you internalise the patterns. After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the 9 U stickers carry no permutation
information.  All the PLL information is the side colouring of the eight
U-layer cubies that sit on the U-slice.

* 4 U-edges.  An U-edge contributes one U sticker and one side sticker
to the cube. 4 × 1 = 4 non-U stickers.
* 4 U-corners.  An U-corner contributes one U sticker and two side
stickers to the cube. 4 × 2 = 8 non-U stickers.

Hence the U-ring, i.e. the whole non-U colouring of the last layer, is

4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12 physical non-U
stickers,

8 distinct U-layer pieces, 4 edges + 4 corners, which is the set that is
normally quoted as the PLL read-out.  The U stickers themselves are
informationless after OLL.

One side colour per cubie is enough to name the cubie, so the
permutation is nominally carried by eight identifiers, four edge side
stickers and four corners.  Up to the C4 rotation about U and the
edge/corner parity of the last layer the eighth cubie is forced, so the
information-theoretic minimum for the permutation is seven independent
non-U identifiers, in sticker terms the familiar 4 edge side stickers +
3 × 2 corner side stickers = 10 physical side stickers, i.e. the
eight-piece, twelve-sticker U-ring.  That is the twelve-sticker,
eight-piece U-slice that is normally spoken of as the PLL information
bearing set, of which seven independent stickers are sufficient in
principle and which in practice is recognised with the much smaller
4–5 sticker glance that is normally used.

reflection_text.6:
The discussion remains a tension between three counts for the U-ring after OLL.

Complete literal set.
After OLL the 9 U stickers are monochromatic and carry no permutation information. The PLL information lives entirely in the side colouring of the 8 U-layer cubies.
* 4 U-edges: 1 non-U sticker per edge → 4 stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 non-U stickers per corner → 8 stickers
Total physical non-U stickers on the U-slice = 4+8 = 12. That is the 8 distinct U-layer pieces normally quoted as the PLL read-out: UF,F ; UR,R ; UB,B ; UL,L and UFR,F,R ; UFL,F,L ; ULB,L,B ; UBR,R,B. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 repeatedly state this 12-sticker / 8-piece set as the whole non-U colouring of the last layer.

Information-theoretic reduction.
Parity and the fixed U colour make the eight pieces not independent. Edge parity = corner parity, so the fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced. In one-identifier-per-cubie language this is 8 identifiers, 7 independent. In physical stickers that is usually expressed as four edge side stickers + three fully identified corners i.e. 4+3×2 =10 physical side stickers, i.e. seven independent non-U stickers. Colleagues 2,4,10,12,6,8 make this explicit.

Practical recognition.
In practice solvers do not inspect the whole ring. The four equatorial edge side stickers visible on two adjacent faces give the edge cycle type. The remaining ambiguity between e.g. G-perms vs U-perms / A-perms is resolved by one well-chosen corner side sticker. Hence a 4-edge +1-corner ≈5-sticker glance is routinely quoted as sufficient for reliable recognition, with parity fixing the last piece. Colleagues 1,7,9,13,14,5 in round 1 now converge on five as the practical minimum, with 1,13,14 explicitly arguing four stickers alone leaves G-perm / E / A-perm overlaps unresolved.

Disagreement.
Colleague 7 in this round reverts to a 4-sticker claim, arguing centres supply corner parity so the four edge side stickers alone determine the 21 cases. That is contested by Colleagues 1,13,14,9 who insist the G-perm family shares edge cycles with U/A perms and needs at least one corner side sticker, i.e. five.

Unresolved for me.
The question can be read as:
* total information-bearing set = 12 non-U stickers, 8 pieces;
* information-theoretic minimum = 7 independent identifiers ≈10 physical stickers;
* practical worst-case glance = 4–5 stickers.
Round 0 and Round 1 both keep the 12-sticker complete literal description as the conventional textbook count, while the 7-independent / 4–5-sticker view is the practical compression. Which reading the question intends – complete literal set vs minimal must-be-seen worst case – is still open, and the split between 4 vs 5 practical stickers remains.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the emerging consensus around five non-top-facing stickers. The four equatorial edge side stickers visible on any two adjacent faces immediately classify the edge permutation (solved, adjacent swap, diagonal swap, or pure swap), while the single additional corner side sticker—most often the UFR or UBR facelet—resolves the only remaining ambiguity, namely the direction of the corner 3-cycle that separates the G-perms from the U- and A-perms. Because edge and corner parities must match, the final piece is then fixed by the known centers without any further information; a sixth sticker is therefore redundant in every one of the 21 cases. Colleagues still citing four stickers correctly note that the edge cycle is visible at a glance, yet overlook the documented G-perm look-alikes that require exactly that fifth sticker to disambiguate from a standard two-face view. This five-sticker pattern is precisely what experienced CFOP solvers use for reliable one-look recognition.

* 4 U-edges : UF,F ; UR,R ; UB,B ; UL,L → 1 non-U side sticker per edge = 4
* 4 U-corners : UFR,F,R ; UFL,F,L ; ULB,L,B ; UBR,B,R → 2 non-U side stickers per corner = 8

4+8 =12 physical non-U stickers, 8 U-layer pieces. Up to C4 rotation about U and edge = corner parity the eighth piece is forced so the permutation is information-theoretically fixed by seven independent non-U identifiers, conventionally quoted as 4 edge side + 3 corners×2 =10 physical stickers.

That 12-sticker, 8-piece U-ring is the complete literal information bearing set of a PLL. The nine U stickers carry no PLL information and the D face and the inner rows of F,R,B,L are never used.

In ordinary one-look CFOP that literal set is compressed. The four equatorial U-edge side stickers visible on any two adjacent side faces give the edge cycle type – solved, adjacent 2-cycle, opposite/diagonal 2-cycle, 3-cycle – with the fixed centres giving the parity reference edge parity = corner parity.

Four edge side stickers alone leave the G-perm family indistinguishable from certain U- and A-perms that share the same edge pattern and leave the corner 3-cycle direction ambiguous. The residual ambiguity is removed by one well chosen corner side sticker, normally UFR or UBR depending on grip.

With 4 U-edge side stickers + 1 U-corner side sticker, i.e. five well chosen non-top stickers, the 21 PLL classes are uniquely named from the standard two-face view and parity + centres forces the last piece. No sixth sticker is ever required in practice.

So the complete literal description is the 12 non-U stickers of the U-ring, 7 independent. The reliable worst-case one-look CFOP glance that separates all 21 cases without rotation is the familiar 4 edge side + 1 corner side ≈ 5 non-top-facing sticker minimum. The four-sticker only claim leaves the documented G-perm vs U/A-perm look-alikes unresolved.
